questions.q: For a regression task predicting a continuous value (like a price), which loss function is the standard choice?
options: nn.CrossEntropyLoss
nn.MSELoss
nn.Softmax
nn.ReLU
questions.explain: nn.MSELoss (mean squared error) is the standard loss for regression tasks where the target is a continuous number, penalizing larger errors disproportionately more via squaring.

questions.q: What shape and content does nn.CrossEntropyLoss expect for its `target` argument in a multi-class classification task?
options: A one-hot encoded vector per example, matching the logits' shape
A tensor of shape (batch_size,) containing the integer class index of the correct class for each example
A tensor of probabilities summing to 1 per example
The same raw logits as the prediction
questions.explain: nn.CrossEntropyLoss expects integer class indices of shape (batch_size,), not one-hot vectors, paired with logits of shape (batch_size, num_classes).

questions.q: Why is it incorrect to apply nn.Softmax to your model's output before passing it to nn.CrossEntropyLoss?
options: Softmax is too slow to compute

nn.CrossEntropyLoss already internally combines a log-softmax and negative-log-likelihood computation in a numerically stable way; pre-applying softmax double-applies the transformation and produces incorrect gradients
Softmax can only be applied to 1-dimensional tensors
It is actually correct and recommended practice
questions.explain: CrossEntropyLoss expects raw logits because it performs log-softmax internally as part of a fused, numerically stable computation. Applying softmax yourself first results in the transformation being applied twice, corrupting the loss and its gradients.

questions.q: What does reduction='mean' (the default) do in nn.MSELoss or nn.CrossEntropyLoss, compared to reduction='sum'?
options: They are functionally identical in all cases
'mean' divides the total loss by the number of elements, keeping the loss scale consistent regardless of batch size; 'sum' adds everything without dividing, so the scale grows with batch size
'mean' only works on GPU; 'sum' only works on CPU
'sum' is required for classification tasks and 'mean' for regression
questions.explain: reduction='mean' normalizes by the number of elements so the loss magnitude doesn't change as batch size changes, keeping training behavior more consistent. reduction='sum' instead totals the per-element losses without normalizing.

questions.q: For binary classification with a single output logit per example, which loss function should you use, and what does it expect as input?
options: nn.MSELoss, expecting probabilities
nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss, expecting a raw logit (not a sigmoid-activated probability)
nn.CrossEntropyLoss, expecting one-hot vectors
nn.Softmax, expecting normalized probabilities
questions.explain: nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss is the binary-classification counterpart to CrossEntropyLoss: it combines a sigmoid and binary cross-entropy in one numerically stable operation, and like CrossEntropyLoss, expects raw logits rather than pre-activated probabilities.
